# Encrypt API gateway traffic on virtual machines

This topic describes how to make TLS certificates available to API gateways so that requests between the user and the gateway endpoint are encrypted.

## Requirements

- Consul v1.15 or later is required to use the Consul API gateway on VMs
  - Consul v1.19 or later is required to use the [file system certificate configuration entry](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/file-system-certificate)
- You must have a certificate and key from your CA
- A Consul cluster with service mesh enabled. Refer to [`connect`](/consul/docs/reference/agent/configuration-file/service-mesh#connect)
- Network connectivity between the machine deploying the API gateway and a
  Consul cluster agent or server

### ACL requirements

If ACLs are enabled, you must present a token with the following permissions to
configure Consul and deploy API gateways:

- `mesh: read`
- `mesh: write`

Refer [Mesh Rules](/consul/docs/security/acl/acl-rules#mesh-rules) for
additional information about configuring policies that enable you to interact
with Consul API gateway configurations.

## Define TLS certificates

1. Create a [file system certificate](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/file-system-certificate) or [inline certificate](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/inline-certificate) and specify the following fields:
   - `Kind`: Specifies the type of configuration entry. This must be set to `file-system-certificate` or `inline-certificate`.
   - `Name`: Specify the name in the [API gateway listener configuration](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/api-gateway#listeners) to bind the certificate to that listener.
   - `Certificate`: Specifies the filepath to the certificate on the local system or the inline public certificate as plain text.
   - `PrivateKey`: Specifies the filepath to private key on the local system or the inline private key to  as plain text.
1. Configure any additional fields necessary for your use case, such as the namespace or admin partition. Refer to the [file system certificate configuration reference](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/file-system-certificate) or [inline certificate configuration reference](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/inline-certificate) for more information.
1. Save the configuration.

### Examples

<Tabs>

<Tab heading="Inline certificate">

The following example defines a certificate named `my-certificate`. API gateway configurations that specify `inline-certificate` in the `Certificate.Kind` field and `my-certificate` in the `Certificate.Name` field are able to use the certificate.

```hcl
Kind = "inline-certificate"
Name = "my-certificate"

Certificate = <<EOF
-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
EOF

PrivateKey = <<EOF
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
...
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
EOF
```

</Tab>

<Tab heading="File system certificate">

The following example defines a certificate named `my-certificate`. API gateway configurations that specify `file-system-certificate` in the `Certificate.Kind` field and `my-certificate` in the `Certificate.Name` field are able to use the certificate.

```hcl
Kind                     = "file-system-certificate"
Name                     = "my-certificate"
Certificate              = "/opt/consul/tls/api-gateway.crt"
PrivateKey               = "/opt/consul/tls/api-gateway.key"
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Deploy the configuration to Consul

Run the `consul config write` command to enable listeners to use the certificate. The following example writes a configuration called `my-certificate.hcl`:

```shell-session
$ consul config write my-certificate.hcl
```

## Terminate TLS with Consul-managed certificates

You can configure the API gateway to terminate downstream TLS with its Consul service mesh leaf certificate instead of a certificate that you provide. Consul issues and rotates the leaf certificate automatically, so you do not need to create a `file-system-certificate` or `inline-certificate` configuration entry.

The leaf certificate is signed by the Consul service mesh certificate authority (CA). Clients that trust the CA root certificate can verify the gateway certificate without additional configuration.

### Requirements for Consul-managed certificates

- Consul v2.1 or later
- A Consul cluster with service mesh enabled. Refer to [`connect`](/consul/docs/reference/agent/configuration-file/service-mesh#connect-parameters)
- To resolve services by name, clients must be able to query [Consul DNS](/consul/docs/discover/dns)

### Certificate DNS names

Consul adds DNS subject alternative names (SANs) to the leaf certificate so that clients can reach each service exposed by the gateway at its `<service>.api-gateway.<domain>` DNS name. Refer to [API gateway service lookups](/consul/docs/discover/service/static#api-gateway-service-lookups) for more information about how Consul registers these names.

The following table describes the wildcard SANs that the leaf certificate includes:

| Services targeted by routes | Wildcard SANs |
| --- | --- |
| Services in the `default` namespace and `default` admin partition | `*.api-gateway.<domain>`<br/>`*.api-gateway.<datacenter>.<domain>` |
| Services in a non-default namespace <EnterpriseAlert inline /> | `*.api-gateway.<namespace>.<domain>`<br/>`*.api-gateway.<namespace>.<datacenter>.<domain>` |
| Services in the `default` namespace of a non-default admin partition <EnterpriseAlert inline /> | `*.api-gateway.<partition>.<domain>`<br/>`*.api-gateway.<partition>.<datacenter>.<domain>` |
| Services in a non-default namespace of a non-default admin partition <EnterpriseAlert inline /> | `*.api-gateway.<namespace>.<partition>.<domain>`<br/>`*.api-gateway.<namespace>.<partition>.<datacenter>.<domain>` |

Consul adds one set of wildcard SANs for each namespace and admin partition that contains a service targeted by a bound route.

The certificate also includes the following SANs:

- The `Hostname` value of each gateway listener, when set.
- The `Hostnames` values of each HTTP route bound to the gateway.
- The equivalent wildcard SANs for the [`alt_domain`](/consul/docs/reference/agent/configuration-file/dns#_alt_domain), when configured.

When you add or remove routes, listeners, or hostnames, Consul reissues the leaf certificate with the updated SANs.

### Enable Consul-managed TLS

Complete the following steps to terminate TLS with the gateway's leaf certificate:

1. Create an API gateway configuration entry and set `TLS.Enabled` to `true`. Do not reference a certificate in the listener `TLS.Certificates` field. The following example configures an HTTP listener on port `8443`:

   <CodeBlockConfig filename="gateway.hcl">

   ```hcl
   Kind = "api-gateway"
   Name = "my-gateway"

   TLS = {
     Enabled = true
   }

   Listeners = [
     {
       Name     = "my-https-listener"
       Port     = 8443
       Protocol = "http"
     }
   ]
   ```

   </CodeBlockConfig>

1. Apply the configuration entry.

   ```shell-session
   $ consul config write gateway.hcl
   ```

1. Bind an HTTP route or TCP route to the listener and create service intentions that allow traffic from the gateway to the destination service. Refer to [Define API gateway routes on virtual machines](/consul/docs/north-south/api-gateway/vm/route) for more information.

`TLS.Enabled` applies to every listener on the gateway. Certificates that you configure on a listener with `TLS.Certificates` or `TLS.SDS` take precedence for requests whose server name indication (SNI) matches the certificate hosts. The leaf certificate serves all other requests. When you configure a gateway-level `TLS.SDS` certificate, the SDS certificate remains the default certificate and the gateway does not serve the leaf certificate. Refer to [`TLS.Enabled`](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/api-gateway#tls-enabled) in the API gateway configuration reference for more information.

### Verify HTTPS traffic

Complete the following steps to verify that the gateway terminates HTTPS with a certificate that clients can trust:

1. Confirm that Consul mapped the service to the gateway. The output includes an entry for the service with `"GatewayKind": "api-gateway"` and the listener port. Refer to [API gateway service mapping](/consul/docs/discover/service/static#api-gateway-service-mapping) for more information.

   ```shell-session
   $ curl --silent $CONSUL_HTTP_ADDR/v1/catalog/gateway-services/my-gateway \
       | jq '[.[] | {Service: .Service.Name, GatewayKind, Port}]'
   ```

1. Resolve the DNS name of the service that the route targets. The A record returns the address of each healthy gateway instance, and the SRV record returns the listener port. The following example resolves the `web` service:

   ```shell-session
   $ dig @127.0.0.1 -p 8600 web.api-gateway.consul A +short
   $ dig @127.0.0.1 -p 8600 web.api-gateway.consul SRV +short
   ```

1. Retrieve the active Consul service mesh CA root certificate. Refer to the [`/connect/ca/roots` API endpoint](/consul/api-docs/connect/ca#list-ca-root-certificates) for more information.

   ```shell-session
   $ curl --silent $CONSUL_HTTP_ADDR/v1/connect/ca/roots \
       | jq --raw-output '.Roots[] | select(.Active) | .RootCert' > consul-ca.pem
   ```

1. Send an HTTPS request to the service through the gateway and verify the certificate with the CA root certificate:

   ```shell-session
   $ curl --cacert consul-ca.pem https://web.api-gateway.consul:8443
   ```

   The request succeeds without the `--insecure` flag because the gateway certificate includes the `*.api-gateway.consul` SAN and chains to the Consul service mesh CA.
